Checking field data with nepstest: what to pay attention to

Source: GUIDELINES.md

This text is for everyone who writes or reviews test scripts with nepstest. It does not repeat the function documentation. Instead it describes the points where mistakes happen easily and where a test can pass or fail for the wrong reason. The getting-started vignette (vignette("nepstest")) explains the task and the functions themselves.

Before you start

Read the field data with haven::read_dta(). This keeps the variable and value labels, which the label tests need, and it leaves the missing codes such as -97 or -98 untouched. Read the PV of the module with read_pv(), so you can look up the tags of each item directly in R.

Keep one script per module and go through the PV in the order of the items. Copy the tag from the PV as a comment directly above each test. This makes it possible for someone else to compare the PV and the script line by line, and it helps you later when the PV changes. When a new delivery comes in, it is usually enough to update the tests of the items that changed since the last delivery, but make sure that changes to a block filter reach every item in that block.

Always use the variable name from the --va: tag. Older PVs sometimes refer to other items by their item number in the filter conditions. Look up the variable name of that item in the PV and use it instead of the number.

Translating filter conditions

The most important point when testing entry filters with ef_test() is how missing values are handled. The CATI and R treat them differently, and a condition that looks correct can silently test the wrong thing.

In the CATI, a condition like “x not equal 2” is also true when x has no value. In R, x != 2 returns NA when x is missing, and ef_test() treats an NA condition as “condition not met”. If you translate the PV literally, every respondent with a missing x is therefore tested against the wrong expectation. The correct translation is !x %in% 2, which is TRUE when x is missing, just as in the CATI. This applies to every condition in the PV that is written as != or <>, and it is one of the most common filter conditions in the PVs, so it is worth checking twice.

For the same reason you should not use == either. Write x %in% 1 instead of x == 1 and x %in% c(1, 2, 4) for a list of values. For conditions on missing values, use is.na(x) for “x = .” and !is.na(x) for “x <> .”.

If ef_test() prints a note that the condition evaluates to NA in some rows, treat this as a sign that the condition was not translated correctly. A correct translation with %in% and is.na() never produces this note.

Comparisons with <, >, <= or >= cannot be written with %in%. Here you have to decide explicitly what happens when the variable is missing, for example !is.na(x) & x > 5. It is not yet confirmed how the CATI treats a missing value in such comparisons, so check this with the person responsible for the PV before relying on such a test.

When an ef-tag has several if lines, they are alternatives: the item is asked if any of them holds. Combine them with | and put each line in brackets, especially when a line itself contains &. An ef-tag at the start of a block applies to every item inside that block, in addition to the item’s own condition. It is easy to forget this, so either add the block condition to every test in the block with &, or filter the data to the block once and run the tests on the filtered data. With nested blocks, the conditions of all enclosing blocks apply.

Reading the results of a filter test

ef_test() checks two things: that the item has a value wherever the condition holds, and that it is empty wherever the condition does not hold. Missing codes like -97 (refused) or -98 (don’t know) count as an answer, because the question was asked. Only an empty value counts as “not asked”.

Failures in the first check are often not programming errors but interviews that were broken off before the item was reached. Look at the printed cases before reporting anything. If many interviews were broken off, it can make sense to run only the second check with check = "not_asked".

Some items are filled automatically without being shown, for example an end date that is set to the interview date when an episode is still ongoing. By default, ef_test() tolerates such values if the duration variable of the item shows that it was not displayed. Keep this in mind when a test passes although you expected a value to be flagged.

Other tests

For autocodings with ac_test(), the data must first be restricted to the rows where the autocoding applies. A test on the unfiltered data fails for rows the autocoding was never meant for. Pass the variables you filtered on as print_filter_vars, so that the printout shows at once why a row failed.

For date ranges with date_test_complex(), keep the order of the arguments in mind: lower limit, upper limit, and only then the dates to be tested. Season codes and missing codes are handled by the function, so you do not need to clean the dates beforehand.

The label tests compare text. Small differences in spelling or formatting are reported as notes and do not make the test fail. Read the notes anyway, since some of them point to real differences.

When a test fails

Every test stops with an error when it finds a problem, so a script run with source() stops at the first failure. Run the script section by section instead.

When a test fails, first check the test itself before you report a problem to the survey institute. Ask yourself whether the condition was translated correctly, especially with regard to missing values, whether the item lies inside a block with its own filter, and whether the PV has changed since the last delivery. Only when the test is right and the printed cases really contradict the PV should the item, the tag and the affected case IDs be reported.
